newsitem.title: USA: Frail Hepburn wants no fuss over 90th birthday.
newsitem.headline: Frail Hepburn wants no fuss over 90th birthday.

text.p: A frail Katharine Hepburn does not want any fuss made over her 90th birthday on May 12, but the rest of the world has other ideas.
The screen legend will be honoured on that day when a New York garden near the United Nations building is dedicated to her, in a ceremony attended by Mayor Rudolph Giuliani.

In addition, U.S. Sen. Joe Lieberman, Democrat of Connecticut, is urging President Bill Clinton to award Hepburn the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and some even think she should be given the Congressional Gold Medal.
Hepburn's birthday will also see the publication by William Morrow and Company of the first comprehensive biography on Hepburn's 26-year affair with actor Spencer Tracy.

"Hepburn deserves the Congressional Gold Medal because she is the symbol of the 20th century American woman," said Christopher Andersen, author of the spicy "An Affair to Remember: The Remarkable Love Story of Katharine Hepburn and Spencer Tracy."
"She is the person who put women in pants, literally and figuratively," Andersen told Reuters in an interview. "She is the greatest star, the greatest actress, that Hollywood has ever produced."
Hartford native Hepburn, who won a record four Academy Awards for Best Actress, lives quietly in the family mansion in the town of Fenwick, Connecticut, overlooking Long Island Sound.

Family members told Reuters Hepburn was not planning any birthday celebration. They said she spends her days gazing out at a lighthouse from her living room, puttering about the house, and going for occasional automobile rides.
"She's doing OK. Her chief problem is loss of memory," her sister-in-law Sue Hepburn said.
Hepburn last year gave up the townhouse on New York's East 49th Street that she had kept since the 1930s and retreated fulltime to the Connecticut shore.
Her last film was "Love Affair" with Warren Beatty several years ago.
"She has suffered a considerable loss of short-term memory, and she doesn't communicate too freely," her brother-in-law Ellsworth Grant said.
"She knows her family and whatnot, but she's kind of withdrawn from the world in general."
But Grant added that Hepburn could possibly survive for a long time in her present state.
"Her body is sound, and she eats well, so this could last for a long time," he said.
Author Andersen, who first met Hepburn in 1976, said she suffered from respiratory problems, but that she did not have Parkinson's disease, as is widely believed because of her famous tremor.
"She's just feeling the effects of a lifetime of gallivanting around. She's really packed a lot in."
Andersen's book focuses on Hepburn's tempestuous relationship with the wildly alcoholic Tracy, who died in 1967.
He said the affair with Tracy, who was married, was what Hepburn cherished above all in her long life. "It lasted a lot longer than most marriages in Hollywood," he said.
Tracy's monogrammed robe still hangs on a hook in Hepburn's bathroom, Andersen said.

The book describes the extent of Tracy's drinking, including his habit of checking into a hotel, stripping naked and sitting in a bathtub for a week of drinking whiskey -- not even bothering to leave the tub to relieve himself.
Yet Andersen argues that Hepburn was by no means a "doormat" for Tracy, as some have contended. He said Hepburn actually "prevailed" in their relationship.
"This is the first person she was really in love with," said the author, who also wrote the Kennedy bestseller, "Jack and Jackie: Portrait of an American Marriage."
Andersen also dismisses lingering rumours that Hepburn was bisexual or lesbian.
"Not true. I investigated that. Kate wore men's suits, and was masculine in some of her gestures...But the fact of the matter is that she's always had a very heterosexual life."
"If she had been gay, she would just tell you. She's not shy."
